positions/apollinarianism/oneLine: In Christ the divine Word took the place of the human rational mind (nous), uniting with a human body and animal soul to form one nature.
positions/apollinarianism/coreClaims/0: Christ is one living, single subject: the divine Word enfleshed.
positions/apollinarianism/coreClaims/1: Two complete natures (each with its own mind) would mean two persons and two sons.
positions/apollinarianism/coreClaims/2: A human mind is changeable and prone to sin; the divine mind in Christ guarantees sinlessness.
positions/apollinarianism/coreClaims/3: ‘One incarnate nature of God the Word’ (a phrase Cyril later adopted, believing it Athanasian).
positions/apollinarianism/origin: Apollinaris (Apollinarius), bishop of Laodicea in Syria and a strong Nicene ally of Athanasius, developed it c. 360–375; condemned by Roman synods (377), Antioch (379) and Constantinople (381).
positions/apollinarianism/strongestArgum: It secures the unity of Christ as one acting subject, avoiding two Sons.
It takes John 1:14 (‘the Word became flesh’, not ‘became a man’) at face value.
positions/apollinarianism/strongestObjec: Gregory of Nazianzus: ‘that which He has not assumed He has not healed’ — the human mind is the seat of sin and must be redeemed.
The Gospels show Christ's human ignorance, growth, fear and choice (Luke 2:52; Mark 13:32; Matthew 26:39).
A Christ without a human mind is not ‘consubstantial with us’ and so not a true example or representative.
positions/apollinarianism/responses/0: Apollinarians replied that Christ's divine mind could still experience human limitation through the flesh.
positions/apollinarianism/responses/1: Some argued that the true image of God in humanity is the Logos-mind, which Christ restores by being it.
positions/apollinarianism/consequences/0: Established the principle of the ‘unassumed is unhealed’, which governs later Christology.
positions/apollinarianism/consequences/1: Apollinarian writings circulated under orthodox names (Athanasius, Julius of Rome), unwittingly shaping Cyril's ‘one nature’ formula.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/name: Antiochene / East Syriac Dyophysitism (called ‘Nestorianism’ by opponents)
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/oneLi: Christ is one person (parsopa / prosopon) in two complete natures, each with its own concrete individuation (qnoma), united without mixture — so that Mary is best called ‘Christotokos’ or ‘Mother of Christ’.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/coreC: Godhead and manhood in Christ are each complete and remain distinct; the impassible Word did not suffer in his divine nature.
The union is a union of good pleasure and of one prosopon — one Lord, one Son, worshipped together.
Divine attributes and human experiences should be ascribed carefully: ‘God was born’ or ‘God died’ is misleading.
(Church of the East, Babai the Great, c. 612) two natures, two qnome, one parsopa of the Son.
The Church of the East has never accepted that it teaches ‘two sons’ or the views condemned at Ephesus.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/origi: Antiochene theology of Diodore of Tarsus and Theodore of Mopsuestia (d. 428), taken up by Nestorius as archbishop of Constantinople (428); condemned at Ephesus (431). The Church of the East in the Persian Empire, honouring Theodore as ‘the Interpreter’, adopted a dyophysite Christology at synods of 484–486 and 612 and through Babai the Great.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/stron: It protects the full, struggling humanity of Jesus that the Gospels and Hebrews depict.
It preserves the impassibility and transcendence of God, avoiding the language of ‘God died’ that seemed to mix Creator and creature.
It anticipated Chalcedon's ‘two natures’ and Leo's Tome; Nestorius himself, reading the Tome late in life (Book of Heraclides), believed it agreed with him.
Many historians argue Nestorius was condemned partly through church politics and Cyril's aggressive tactics.
Cyril: if the subject of Christ's sufferings is not God the Word, then a mere man died for us and Christ is divided into two sons.
Rejecting Theotokos implies that the one born of Mary was not God — contradicting John 1:14.
A union ‘of good pleasure’ looks like the indwelling of a saint, differing only in degree.
Chalcedonians and Miaphysites alike reject the Church of the East's veneration of Theodore and Nestorius.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/respo: East Syriac theologians answer that ‘one parsopa’ means a true single Son and that they never taught two sons.
The 1994 Common Christological Declaration with Rome recognised that the Assyrian Church confesses the same faith in different terms, accepting ‘Mother of Christ our God and Saviour’.
Scholars note that Syriac qnoma does not mean ‘person’, so ‘two qnome’ is not ‘two persons’.
positions/east-syriac-dyophysitism/conse: The Church of the East became the great missionary church of Asia: Persia, Arabia, India (Saint Thomas Christians), Central Asia, Mongolia and Tang China (Xi'an Stele, 781).
Its separation from the Roman-Byzantine church spared it imperial suspicion in Persia.
‘Nestorian’ became a pejorative label; the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church are its heirs today.
positions/eutychianism/oneLine: Christ was ‘of two natures’ before the union but has only one nature after it, his humanity being absorbed into or transformed by the divinity, so that his body is not consubstantial with ours.
positions/eutychianism/coreClaims/0: After the incarnation there is one nature only.
positions/eutychianism/coreClaims/1: Christ's humanity is not of the same essence as ours (Eutyches at the Synod of Constantinople, 448).
positions/eutychianism/coreClaims/2: To speak of two natures after the union is Nestorian.
positions/eutychianism/origin: Eutyches, an elderly archimandrite in Constantinople and fierce anti-Nestorian, condemned by Patriarch Flavian (448), restored by the Second Council of Ephesus (449), condemned at Chalcedon (451). Later rejected also by Miaphysite leaders such as Timothy Aelurus and Severus.
positions/eutychianism/strongestArgument: It appeared to be the logical extreme of Cyril's insistence on one subject.
It honours the transfiguring power of the divine over flesh.
positions/eutychianism/strongestObjectio: If Christ's humanity is not consubstantial with ours, he is not our representative and cannot heal our nature.
Rejected by Chalcedonians and Miaphysites alike — Oriental Orthodox churches anathematise Eutyches.
Contradicts the Gospel accounts of Christ's real hunger, fatigue and death.
positions/eutychianism/responses/0: Eutyches' supporters argued he meant only to deny a separate human person, and that he was a poor theologian rather than a heretic.
positions/eutychianism/consequences/0: Precipitated Leo's Tome and the Council of Chalcedon.
positions/eutychianism/consequences/1: The label ‘Monophysite’ was later applied polemically to Miaphysites, who reject Eutyches.
positions/miaphysitism/oneLine: Christ is one incarnate nature of God the Word — one united divine-human nature, from two, without mixture, confusion or alteration — in which full divinity and full humanity remain real.
positions/miaphysitism/coreClaims/0: Following Cyril: ‘one incarnate nature (mia physis) of God the Word’.
positions/miaphysitism/coreClaims/1: Christ is from two natures, but after the union one cannot speak of ‘two natures’ as if two acting subjects.
positions/miaphysitism/coreClaims/2: His humanity is complete and consubstantial with ours; divinity and humanity are not mixed (Eutyches is anathematised).
positions/miaphysitism/coreClaims/3: Chalcedon's ‘in two natures’ and Leo's Tome reintroduce Nestorian division.
positions/miaphysitism/coreClaims/4: The one Word incarnate suffered in the flesh; Mary is Theotokos.
positions/miaphysitism/origin: Rooted in Cyril of Alexandria; Dioscorus of Alexandria (deposed at Chalcedon, 451); theologically developed by Timothy Aelurus, Philoxenus of Mabbug and above all Severus of Antioch (d. 538); church structures rebuilt by Jacob Baradaeus. The Armenian Church rejected Chalcedon formally in the 6th century (Dvin, 506 and 554).
positions/miaphysitism/strongestArgument: It is the faithful continuation of Cyril and of the Council of Ephesus, which Chalcedon itself claimed to follow.
It secures that the one who suffered and died is God the Word himself — the basis of salvation.
Before Chalcedon, ‘physis’ was often used to mean a concrete individual; ‘one nature’ therefore meant ‘one Christ’, not a mixture.
The Ethiopian word Tewahedo (‘made one’) expresses the unity that the Oriental churches see as the heart of the gospel.
positions/miaphysitism/strongestObjectio: Chalcedonians argue ‘one nature’ obscures the abiding distinctness of the humanity and risks Eutychian absorption.
Leo and later Chalcedonians held that two natures, each acting in communion with the other, are required for Christ to be truly consubstantial with us.
The rejection of Chalcedon divided the church at a time of external threat (Persian and Arab invasions).
positions/miaphysitism/responses/0: Miaphysites point out that they condemn Eutyches and affirm Christ's humanity as complete and unconfused.
positions/miaphysitism/responses/1: Modern agreed statements (1989–90) accepted that both sides confess the same faith with different terminology, each rejecting Nestorian and Eutychian extremes.
positions/miaphysitism/responses/2: They note that Chalcedonians themselves added Cyrilline clarifications at Constantinople II (553).
positions/miaphysitism/consequences/0: The Oriental Orthodox churches — Coptic, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac, Malankara — form a distinct communion of roughly 60 million people.
positions/miaphysitism/consequences/1: Under Arab rule after the 630s, Miaphysite churches survived as large Christian minorities; the Ethiopian church became a national church.
positions/miaphysitism/consequences/2: Long-standing estrangement from Chalcedonian churches, now eased by dialogue and common declarations (Paul VI and Shenouda III, 1973).
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/oneL: One and the same Christ, Son, Lord, only-begotten, is acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, the properties of each preserved and concurring in one person (hypostasis).
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/core: Christ is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, consubstantial with the Father as to Godhead and with us as to manhood.
The two natures remain distinct after the union, each with its properties, united in one hypostasis (the hypostatic union).
The one person is the eternal Word; Mary is Theotokos.
Communicatio idiomatum: what belongs to either nature may be predicated of the one person (‘the Lord of glory was crucified’).
(Constantinople III, 681) Christ has two natural wills and two energies, the human freely subject to the divine.
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/orig: Defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451), drawing on Cyril's letters, the Formula of Reunion (433) and Leo's Tome; interpreted in a Cyrilline direction at Constantinople II (553) and completed by Constantinople III (681). Received by Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Reformed churches; Lutheran and Reformed later differed over the communication of attributes.
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/stro: It holds together all the biblical data: Christ's full deity and full humanity in one subject.
Its four negative adverbs set boundaries against both Nestorian division and Eutychian confusion, without claiming to explain the mystery.
It reconciled the best of Alexandria (one subject) and Antioch and Rome (two complete natures).
It has been received by the large majority of Christians for 1,500 years.
Miaphysites: ‘in two natures’ sounds like two subjects; Leo's Tome seems to make each nature an actor.
The Church of the East: it confuses by insisting on one hypostasis and Theotokos, compromising divine impassibility.
Modern critics: its static Greek categories (nature, substance) cannot do justice to a historical, personal Jesus (e.g. Schleiermacher, Harnack).
It was enforced by emperors and caused centuries of schism in Egypt and Syria.
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/resp: Chalcedonians stress that the definition explicitly confesses ‘one and the same’ Son, and that Constantinople II clarified its Cyrilline meaning.
Defenders argue that the definition is a ‘grammar’ of boundaries rather than a speculative theory, compatible with modern historical study.
Agreed statements with Oriental Orthodox and Assyrian churches suggest the disagreements were largely terminological.
positions/chalcedonian-dyophysitism/cons: Basis of Christology in Catholic, Eastern Orthodox and Protestant confessions.
Its rejection created the Oriental Orthodox communion; imperial efforts at reunion produced further controversies (Henotikon, Three Chapters, monothelitism).
Shaped Reformation debates (Lutheran ubiquity vs Reformed ‘extra Calvinisticum’) about Christ's presence in the Eucharist.
